human_tolerance.notes: Adaptable to many habitats and considered a generalist species. Will use bat houses for their roosts, and landowners purchase or construct bat houses to attract them because the species is agriculturally valuable, feeding on cucumber beetles and other crop pests.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Big brown bat mating season is in the fall, shortly before annual hibernation. Females are pregnant through the winter and give birth after hibernation ends in the spring.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: Annual hibernation in caves, mines and tunnels. Big brown bats are relatively resistant to white-nose syndrome: even in caves harbouring Pseudogymnoascus destructans they maintain normal torpor patterns and retain more body fat through hibernation than more affected species.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: After hibernation ends, pregnant females separate into maternity colonies, which range from 5 to 700 individuals and are frequently 25-75 adults in the eastern US and Canada. Oftentimes only one offspring is produced per litter, though twins are common in the Eastern US.

vocalizations.description: A high-frequency sonar call emitted into the environment, with the bat listening to the returning echoes. Echolocation lets the species determine how far away an object is, its size, shape and density, and the direction in which it is moving.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives family Vespertilionidae, order Chiroptera and authority (Palisot de Beauvois, 1796); ITIS scientific-name search returns TSN 180008 with the same authority. Palisot de Beauvois described it as Vespertila fuscus from specimens in the Philadelphia Museum of Charles Willson Peale.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 2432352 from species/match; ITIS TSN 180008 from the ITIS scientific-name search; NCBI taxon id 29078 and IUCN category least concern (Q211005) from Wikidata P685 and P141.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005), and the source states the species 'is not considered at risk for extinction, and is evaluated as the lowest conservation priority by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)'.

range.note: 'The big brown bat occurs widely throughout the US, Canada, Central America, and the Caribbean. Its range extends into parts of South America, found as far south as Colombia and Venezuela.' The Central American and Caribbean country list is the described range rather than a per-country breakdown, so it is recorded at country level and read as approximate.

traits.limb_count.note: Four limbs: two hind legs of 10 mm and the two forelimbs modified as wings, the uropatagium being the flight membrane between the hind limbs.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Fly and Glide are the bat's own means of movement and the source describes the species as flying and foraging at night. Climb is included for the roosting and crawling behaviour the source records, since big brown bats 'generally roost in cavities, though they can sometimes be found under exfoliating bark' and hang from cave and structure roofs. No trot, gallop or walk is claimed: the schema has no bat-specific crawl and a bat on the ground is not a walker.

traits.skin.note: Furred: 'Its dorsal fur is reddish brown and glossy in appearance; its ventral fur is lighter brown', while the snout, uropatagium and wing membranes are black and hairless.

traits.nest_type.note: Cavity: the species roosts in 'mines, caves, tunnels, buildings, bat boxes, tree cavities, storm drains, wood piles, and rock crevices' and 'generally roost in cavities'. It builds no constructed nest, so the cavity is both roost and nursery.

traits.perching.note: Authored: bats hang from the ceilings of their roosts, so a hanging roost is the bat's equivalent of a perch and the perched pose is used for it. The source describes the roosting habit but uses the word perch of no animal, so this is an interpretation of the roosting posture.

traits.senses.note: hearing High from the echolocation described in detail in the source, which resolves object distance, size, shape, density and movement. night_vision false is an authored judgement: the source attributes the species' night foraging to echolocation rather than to vision, and says echolocation 'allows them to occupy a niche where there are often many insects (that come out at night since there are fewer predators then), less competition for food, and fewer species that may prey on the big brown bat itself'. olfaction Med is authored, with no sourced claim found.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.01698 kg falls in the Tiny band, under 0.05 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: Mean of EltonTraits MamFuncDat BodyMass-Value 16.46 g and PanTHERIA AdultBodyMass_g 17.49 g, giving 0.01698 kg, inside the source's 15-26 g range.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the adult body length 110-130 mm, which the source gives separately from the 47-52 mm tail, so this is head-and-body length rather than total length.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-Inv 100, matching 'Big brown bats are insectivorous, consuming a diverse array of insects, particularly night-flying insects, but especially beetles', including crop pests such as the cucumber beetle.

traits.social.note: Colony: 'Maternity colonies range in size from 5-700 individuals, though in the eastern US and Canada, they are frequently 25-75 adults', and in summer 'males are most often solitary, though they may form small, all-male colonies'. The lower bound of 1 records the solitary male and solitary non-pregnant female; the upper bound of 700 is the sourced maximum colony size.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'The big brown bat is nocturnal, roosting in sheltered places during the day', foraging for prey at night.

traits.defense.note: Authored: the species' documented response to disturbance is to fly, and the source notes it is among the bats least affected by white-nose syndrome, so it is not a weak or dying animal. No sourced statement describes an aggressive defence, so Flee is recorded.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: a nocturnal animal that roosts in human structures and bat boxes by choice, so it neither avoids nor seeks people out; a middling value is used.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-Value 'A' gives the primary stratum as aerial. The arboreal share of 0.3 is authored judgement for the tree-cavity, bark and structure roosting the source describes.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'They generally roost in cavities', in tree cavities, buildings, caves, mines, tunnels, bat boxes, storm drains, wood piles and rock crevices.

habitat.resources.note: invertebrate carries the full share and follows traits.diet. The cavity and perch weights are an authored 0.6/0.4 split of the roosting resource between the cavity itself and the hanging position within it, because the source describes both and does not weigh them; no open source quantifies their relative use.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'It is adaptable to many habitats and is considered a generalist species'; 'Big brown bats are a species that will use bat houses for their roosts. Landowners will purchase or construct bat houses and install them, hoping to attract big brown bats'; the species is the official state mammal of the District of Columbia.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'Their breeding season is in the fall, shortly before their annual hibernation. After hibernation ends in the spring, females form maternity colonies for giving birth to young.' The animal is a hibernating insectivore, not a year-round or migrant one.

seasonal.triggers.note: Authored thresholds, and an honest gap: the source states that the species hibernates annually and that breeding precedes it, but gives no temperature or day-length threshold for entering or leaving hibernation, and none was found in an openly licensed source. The enter value of 5 degrees C for 14 days and the exit value of 10 degrees C for 14 days are order-of-magnitude judgements for a temperate insectivorous bat, chosen to be consistent with the source's sequence of autumn mating, winter hibernation and spring maternity colonies. Treat them as placeholders; the 14-day persistence requirement is included so the simulation does not trigger on a single cold or warm day.

seasonal.phases.note: Mating window from 'Big brown bat mating season is in the fall, shortly before their annual hibernation'; dormancy from the same sentence plus the resistance to white-nose syndrome described under the same section; nesting window from 'After hibernation ends in the spring, pregnant females separate into maternity colonies' with colony sizes and litter sizes. Exact window edges are judgements informed by those dates.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Authored: the source gives litter size ('Oftentimes only one offspring is produced per litter, though twins are common in the Eastern US') but no birth weight, weaning age or age at first flight, so the 60-day juvenile duration and the 0.4 scale are both judgements. No egg stage is listed because bat young are born as developed young rather than eggs.

vocalizations.echolocation.note: From the Behavior section: 'Like many other species of microbats, the big brown bat often uses echolocation to navigate. This means that the species emits a call out into its environment and listens to the echoes of those calls that return from various objects near them. Using echolocation, big brown bats can determine how far away an object is, the objects size, shape and density, and the direction (if any) that an object is moving.' The call_id is authored; the context Buzz is the schema's term for a continuous tonal call and no source assigns a context.

vocalizations.note: The description is sourced; the single entry exists because the schema requires a vocalization and the source describes only the echolocation call, naming no social or alarm vocalisation. The time window and cooldown are authored judgement, since no open source quantifies them. No frequency band is given in the source, so freq_hz is deliberately omitted rather than filled with a typical bat frequency from memory.

look.note: Colours from the Description section: 'Its dorsal fur is reddish brown and glossy in appearance; its ventral fur is lighter brown. Its snout, uropatagium (flight membrane between the hind limbs), and wing membranes are black and hairless. Its ears (12-13 millimetres) are also black; they are relatively short with rounded tips.' The beak slot carries the black snout, the wings and tail the black hairless membranes, and the breast the lighter ventral fur; small extra ear parts render the short rounded ears. One honest caveat is recorded in the body-plan provenance: a bat is a mammal, not a bird, and the biped_winged plan is the only body plan in the kit with wing parts and working flight animation, so it is used for the model and the legs are drawn short to sit closer to a bat's proportions than a bird's.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program, chosen because it is the only shared program with a night-time resting window and a food-search state, which suits a nocturnal insectivore. food_tag set to invertebrate, the whole diet. flee_m 15 m and calm_m 30 m reflect an animal that leaves a roost and does not approach a person. food_m 50 m is a long foraging radius, matching a bat that ranges widely at night to catch night-flying insects. rest_sun_lo_deg 12 and rest_sun_hi_deg 90 are authored for a strictly nocturnal species, roosting while the sun is up. The program's gaits are walk for both flee and forage because its gait vocabulary has no flight term, even though this species moves by flying; that mismatch is left visible rather than hidden.
